stem: A newborn is found to have a ventricular septal defect on echocardiography but no murmur is heard on day 1; what is the best explanation?

options.text: A VSD murmur may not be apparent until pulmonary vascular resistance falls over the first 6 weeks
A VSD murmur only appears once the ductus venosus closes at 3 to 7 days
A VSD murmur is absent in infancy because left ventricular dominance is already established at birth
A VSD murmur cannot be heard until adulthood because neonatal right ventricular dominance persists permanently
A VSD murmur is only expected if the foramen ovale remains patent in adulthood

explanation: A VSD murmur may be absent at birth because pulmonary vascular resistance is still high, so there may be little left-to-right shunting until it falls over the first 6 weeks of life.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Correct because a VSD murmur may not be heard initially while pulmonary vascular resistance remains high, and it becomes more apparent as resistance falls over the first 6 weeks.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because delayed VSD murmur appearance is related to falling pulmonary vascular resistance, not ductus venosus closure.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because newborns have relatively high pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular dominance, not established left ventricular dominance at birth.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because VSD murmurs can become audible in infancy as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; they do not wait until adulthood.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because a patent foramen ovale in adulthood is unrelated to the timing of a VSD murmur.
